title: Bangladesh blames Awami League for arson wave as Hasina vows December return
dek: Police link bus burnings and dozens of crude-bomb blasts to the banned party of Sheikh Hasina, who is in India. Dhaka wants her extradited; Delhi says it will follow 'the appropriate legal process'. The Ganga water treaty expires on 12 December.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh has been hit by a wave of bus burnings and crude-bomb blasts since last weekend, which police blame on the banned Awami League of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who has said she will return from exile in India in December. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government has refused her a passport and wants India to hand her over, putting New Delhi at the centre of a crisis that is building just as the India-Bangladesh treaty on sharing the Ganga's waters is due to expire on 12 December.

India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Tuesday that any extradition request would be dealt with "through the appropriate legal process". The violence has killed at least one person, a bus driver who died of smoke inhalation when his bus was set alight in Faridpur, according to reports.

## What happened

Bangladesh's Police Headquarters said 19 buses were torched and crude bombs went off at 29 places between Saturday 7 November and Monday 9 November, according to reports. It said 29 people had been arrested and 11 cases filed. From Monday to Tuesday, another 22 vehicles were burned in 11 districts and crude bombs exploded at no fewer than 28 locations in Dhaka and six other districts, one report said. Figures from the Dhaka Metropolitan Police showed 49 crude-bomb blasts in the capital over three days, according to another. The figures come from police and have not been independently verified; reports differ on how many districts have been affected.

Police in Dhaka said they had arrested 33 people in the capital. A Dhaka Metropolitan Police official, Akhter Hossain, said "almost 99 percent of those arrested are linked to the Awami League and its associate organisations". The Awami League, which has been banned under Bangladesh's Anti-Terrorism Act since 10 April 2025, had not issued a formal response to the accusations by Thursday.

The Inspector General of Police, Ali Hossain Fakir, told the superintendents of all 64 districts to make "quality arrests", meaning the people actually responsible rather than mass detentions, according to reports. Six platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh were deployed in Gopalganj, the Awami League's heartland, after a rally in Tungipara, Hasina's ancestral home, where a police vehicle was burned, reports said.

## The passport and the extradition demand

On Monday, a London law firm, Matrix Chambers, wrote to Bangladesh's High Commission in New Delhi asking it to issue Hasina a new passport and national identity card, according to reports. The mission said it could not verify the firm's authority to act for her. Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Humaiun Kobir, called the request "utterly ridiculous" and again called Hasina a "terrorist", reports said.

Bangladesh's chief prosecutor at the International Crimes Tribunal, Md Aminul Islam, has said Hasina missed the 30-day window to appeal against her conviction and that her sentence would be carried out if she returned, according to reports. The tribunal sentenced her in absentia last November to death on one charge and to life imprisonment on another, for crimes against humanity during the crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising. She denies the charges.

Asked about the request at the MEA's weekly briefing on Tuesday, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said extradition would be handled "through the appropriate legal process" and added: "For travel of people, you need a travel document." On the passport and identity card, he said: "This is a matter they [the Bangladesh High Commission] would be in a better position to respond to." He said there was no new update on talks about the Ganga water treaty or on a visit to India by Prime Minister Rahman, according to reports of the briefing.

Hasina, 79, told an international news agency in an interview published on Wednesday that fear could not decide her duty to her people. She said she was fully aware that she could face execution and that India was not putting pressure on her to return or to stay.

## Background

Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as protests against her 15-year rule turned into an uprising. Dhaka first asked India to extradite her in December 2024. The interim government led by Muhammad Yunus banned the Awami League in April 2025, and the party was kept out of the general election of 12 February 2026, in which the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won 209 seats and Jamaat-e-Islami 68. Tarique Rahman, who returned from 17 years in exile in December 2025, became prime minister.

Relations with India have been uneasy since. A planned visit to India by Rahman fell through in August, and he did not attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September, according to reports. Dhaka has made a speedier decision on Hasina's extradition a condition for any visit, reports said.

## What they are saying

At a meeting of BNP members of parliament on Monday, Rahman told them to "remain on the streets", according to reports, and Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the Awami League would never return. Jamaat-e-Islami's secretary general, Mia Golam Porwar, said the government had "completely failed" to maintain order, and a leader of the National Citizen Party (NCP), Sarwar Tushar, said the home minister could not keep order even in his own constituency, reports said.

The Awami League says its leader is the victim of a political trial. Hasina has called the tribunal's case a "jurisprudential joke".

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

India is holding the one person the government in Dhaka most wants. A decision to extradite her would break with India's long ties to the Awami League; a refusal, or a return that India is seen to have allowed, would deepen the strain with an elected government that India has said it wants "constructive" relations with.

The timing matters for West Bengal in particular. The 1996 Ganga Water Sharing Treaty, which divides the river's dry-season flow at the Farakka barrage between 1 January and 31 May, expires on 12 December, and no renewal has been announced. Under the treaty, each country is guaranteed 35,000 cusecs in alternating 10-day periods between 11 March and 10 May, and the two governments must consult if the flow at Farakka falls below 50,000 cusecs. Because water is a state subject, a new treaty needs West Bengal's agreement; Dhaka wants a guarantee clause on minimum flows. Unrest in the run-up to December would also be watched closely along West Bengal's 2,217-km border with Bangladesh, the longest of any Indian state.

## What happens next

- The BNP has said its supporters will stay on the streets through December, which Bangladesh marks as Victory Month.
- Hasina has said she will return in December; she has not said how, without a passport.
- India has not said whether it will act on Dhaka's extradition request.
- The Ganga Water Sharing Treaty expires on 12 December; no date has been announced for talks to renew it.

## Timeline

- 7-10 November 2026: bus burnings and crude-bomb blasts across Bangladesh; police blame the Awami League.
- 9 November 2026: lawyers ask Bangladesh's mission in Delhi to issue Hasina a passport.
- 10 November 2026: MEA says extradition will follow "the appropriate legal process".
- 12 December 2026: Ganga Water Sharing Treaty expires.
